title: High Court's coalmine emissions ruling says 'the quiet part out loud'
text:
Resources company MACH Energy probably never expected its high court appeal over the future of a Hunter Valley coal mine to trigger a legal precedent that has been celebrated by climate activists.

The court's decision has the resources sector nervous, the federal government downplaying the ruling's wider significance, and the opposition apoplectic about its potential to cripple the Australian fossil fuel industry.

The extension of the Mount Pleasant coalmine would add roughly twice Australia's total annual greenhouse gas emissions to the atmosphere. (Supplied: Nearmaps)

Whether the ruling is a narrow interpretation of a planning statute or spells doom for the fossil fuel industry depends on who you talk to.

So, let's step through it all carefully.

What was the case about?

MACH Energy operates the Mount Pleasant open-cut mine near Muswellbrook.

It wants to double the amount of coal it exports from the mine and keep it open until 2048.

NSW's Independent Planning Commission (IPC) approved that expansion in 2022. But the plan came to a dramatic halt when a residents' group convinced the state's Court of Appeal the IPC got it wrong.

The Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMSHEG), led by two retired schoolteachers, said the planning panel failed to properly consider that climate change caused by the exported coal's "downstream" or scope 3 emissions would cause harm to the Hunter.

'Dangerous loophole' in the law In a week of floods and droughts across Australia, the government extended the life of one of the world's largest gas facilities.

What are scope 3 emissions?

Under climate regulations, Scope 1 emissions are those that come from the source, such as methane leaks from a coalmine.

Scope 2 emissions are caused by electricity that has been generated using fossil fuels.

Scope 3 emissions are indirect emissions, and in this case describe the "downstream" or "chain emissions" that occur when a product is sold on and used — in this case, when the exported coal is burned overseas.

Globally, they account for the vast majority of emissions from coalmines and other fossil fuel production.

In July 2025, the NSW Court of Appeal agreed with DAMSHEG's argument.

It found none of the IPC's conditions expressly addressed scope 3 emissions, despite it being a legal requirement to "ensure greenhouse gas emissions are minimised to the greatest extent possible".

The court sent the case to be reviewed again, this time by the Land and Environment Court.

Frustrated with the delays, and in an effort to get some clear guidance on a path forward, the coal company took its case to the High Court, which agreed to review the planning process.

MACH Energy wants to extract more than 440 million tonnes of coal from the site. (Supplied: Climate Media Centre)

University of Melbourne expert Professor Jacqueline Peel said it was a "very unusual case" for the High Court to take up.

She described the case as "largely an issue of statutory interpretation, what the words of the statute meant".

"On one take it's a just a narrow decision interpreting a specific provision or provisions of New South Wales planning law," she said.

Jacqueline Peel is an expert in environmental and climate change law. (Supplied)

What did the High Court find?

In its original approval, the IPC accepted that 860 million tonnes of emissions would be generated overseas from the project, and that this would contribute to climate change.

But the planning panel said that "would be accounted for" by the countries that imported the coal, "through broader national policies and international agreements (such as the Paris Agreement)".

On the hook for fossil fuel exports The International Court of Justice was unequivocal about the consequences for countries that make the climate crisis worse. As one of the world's biggest fossil fuel exporters, it puts Australia on notice.

MACH Energy's appeal to the High Court argued the same: that the Paris Agreement was enough, and that essentially once the coal left Australia, it was not the company's problem.

But the High Court dismissed that argument in a majority 3 to 2 ruling.

The court found NSW law required the IPC to "consider imposing conditions to minimise to the greatest extent practicable all greenhouse gas emissions, including Scope 3 emissions".

What does it mean for fossil fuel projects?

Professor Peel said at its most narrow reading, the High Court ruling essentially enforced NSW planning law that already existed.

But she said the potential big change was that the High Court was now "saying the quiet part out loud".

"If you start requiring mines to actually deal with and be accountable for their scope 3 emissions and have to do something to minimise those, then it makes the coal mine a much different economic prospect than it would be if you can just deal with scope 3 emissions as someone else's problem," she said.

The Australian Conservation Foundation's Adam Bandt said the outcome was something governments and corporations had long been fighting against.

"There came a time when we understood that asbestos was a product that when you used it as intended would cause harm," Mr Bandt said.

"That's now the same with coal and gas. We don't mine and export asbestos anymore."

The Minerals Council's Tanya Constable said she was "very concerned about the decision".

"This will send shudders down everybody's spine," she said.

MACH Energy's Mount Pleasant coal mine can continue operating until the end of 2032. (7.30 Report)

It is the requirement to consider emissions overseas, not just those happening in Australia, that has the industry and conservative politicians so worked up.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said it was "absurd" to ask local planning authorities to consider climate impacts in other countries before approving a mine in New South Wales.

"Under the international rules … emissions are counted where coal is used, not where it is mined," he said.

But those rules appear to be changing.

In July 2025, the International Court of Justice issued an advisory opinion putting accountability for climate-related harm onto coal and other fossil fuel producers at the point of extraction.

The UK Supreme Court also ruled that the future impact of fossil fuel projects must be assessed by planning bodies when deciding whether to approve projects.

High Court Judge Gordon appeared to accept this argument in her own findings from the MACH Energy case.

"The impact of greenhouse gas emissions is the same, regardless of how they are categorised," Judge Gordon found.

The fact that scope 3 emissions were accounted for by other countries through the Paris Agreement did "not address the Commission's obligation … which relates to all greenhouse gas emissions (including Scope 3 emissions), and which requires it to consider imposing conditions to minimise to the greatest extent practicable those emissions".

Advocates for climate action attend the International Court of Justice decision in 2025. (Supplied: Ray Campbell / Pacific Community)

What's next?

Both the NSW and federal governments have downplayed the broader significance of the ruling.

NSW Premier Chris Minns warned climate activists not to "get overexcited" and said the mine's operators were still "looking to continue an application through the IPC" to expand the mine.

Federal Industry Minister Tim Ayres said the High Court decision was "not a big deal" and "confined to the provisions of the NSW Act and the way that the NSW planning authority did their work".

Workers from Hunter Valley Operations coal mine attend an IPC hearing. (ABC Upper Hunter: Courtney Yeandle)

But Professor Peel said that was a "narrow" interpretation of the ruling.

"It's entirely understandable that the minister at the federal level would be trying to say: 'No, this is just a NSW problem,'" she said.

"But I just don't think we've had that argument in the court yet."

She said she expected new litigation to result from the decision.

"Groups will now want to explore what that added set of arguments from the High Court decision might offer in terms of challenging approvals for fossil fuel projects," she said.

title: Biggest coal-producing state fears impact of High Court emissions decision
text:
A High Court ruling that planning authorities needed to take overseas emissions into account when approving projects could spook investors, the industry fears.

Yesterday, the High Court ruled in favour of a New South Wales community group which had been fighting the expansion of a coal mine in the Hunter Valley region.

The court ruled the state's planning body had failed to consider the emissions of coal burnt overseas when approving the project.

The High Court yesterday ruled in favour of a community group which fought to block an expansion of a coal mine in New South Wales. (Supplied: Zoe Lonergan)

Speaking to the ABC, federal industry minister Tim Ayres was quick to downplay broader impacts, saying it was "squarely a NSW decision", which would be worked through by the state government.

He stressed there would not be implications for either jobs or investment in the sector.

"It is a High Court decision, but it's absolutely confined to the provisions of the New South Wales Act and the way … the planning authority did their work," he told the ABC.

Resources minister Madeline King agreed it was a "pretty technical ruling" which she believed would not impact other states unless their planning legislation contained similar provisions.

Queensland Premier David Crisafulli says the state is "open for business" when it comes to investment in mining. (ABC News: Brendan Mounter)

Premier says Queensland laws 'bulletproof'

In Queensland, Australia's largest coal producing state, Premier David Crisafulli sought to allay industry fears, saying the state's "already bulletproof" laws would be amended if needed in response to the ruling.

"We have the best laws in the country, and we have the highest environmental standards and we are the most pro-mining government in the nation," he said.

The state's peak industry association for the resources sector feels the ruling could have further-reaching impacts.

Overseas emissions, known as 'scope three' emissions, are already considered by regulators, according to the Environmental Protection Act.

Brisbane-based environmental activist Ellen Roberts welcomed the New South Wales ruling.

She said it was important for decision makers to take these emissions into account because they impacted not only people overseas but people in Australia.

But Queensland Resources Council chief executive Janette Hewson said she was concerned by any changes to the interpretation of laws and regulation because it increased risk in the sector.

Janette Hewson is the chief executive of the Queensland Resources Council. (ABC News: Erin Byrnes)

"We are very concerned that our international partners, whether they're investors or customers, will look at what's been happening in Australia," she said.

" This is just the tip of the iceberg in terms of the challenges our industry faces. "

'Shudder down everyone's spine'

Those concerns were echoed by the Minerals Council of Australia — the group going as far as to say the ruling would send "shudder's down everyone's spine" in the industry.

Qld parliament to debate mining law changes Proposed laws in Queensland would restrict who can object to a mine.

Its chief executive Tanya Constable described herself as "very concerned", and although she conceded the decision affected New South Wales, said it would set a "bad precedent" in other jurisdictions.

The MCA's concerned the decision would spook investors, leading them to fund overseas projects rather than in Australia.

Queensland senator Matt Canavan was even more scathing, imploring "all governments" to overturn the High Court's decision by passing laws through state or federal parliaments.

He said it was "ridiculous" to have a situation where the viability of Australian mining projects, as well as jobs, were threatened because of emissions created overseas.

Professor John Rolfe said it could be hypocritical for Australian mining projects to have to take overseas emissions into account. (Supplied: CQ University)

Regional economic development expert John Rolfe at Central Queensland University agreed further applying that scope three standard could be "very disruptive" to the industry and the state's economy.

"It would scare off investors because it would increase costs," he explained.

"Industry are watching it really closely because if you look in Queensland, the coal industry is really important."

title: Dropped Aussie opener out of Sheffield Shield match with concussion
text:
Jake Weatherald's wretched run has continued, with the discarded Test opener forced out of the start of the domestic cricket season with concussion.

Weatherald was subbed out of South Australia's opening game against Victoria at Junction Oval on Thursday, before the start of day two.

He crashed into the picket fence while chasing the ball on Wednesday during Victoria's first innings.

Weatherald then faced only faced six balls at the end of day one before Victorian debutant Harry Hoekstra had him caught behind for a duck.

It is understood Weatherald had delayed symptoms, prompting the decision on Thursday morning to take him out of the game.

Matthew Gilkes took Weatherald's place in the SA line-up.

Weatherald was dropped from the Test team in August after their shock first-Test loss to Bangladesh in Darwin.

Hoekstra also top-scored with 45 at number nine as Victoria rallied to reach 244 in their first innings.

South Australia resumed at 1-4 and were 5-185 approaching tea.

Opener Henry Hunt made 71 before David Moody bowled him in a crucial breakthrough for the fourth wicket.

Jake Lehmann was 52 not out and Hoekstra had continued his fine debut with three wickets.

AAP

title: 'Live on forever': Brock inspires Bathurst 20 years on
text:
Just as he does every year, Craig Lowndes is drawing on memories of Australian motorsport legend Peter Brock to fuel yet another attempt at the Bathurst 1000.

It is just that this year's Great Race feels a bit more special, with Australian motorsport marking 20 years since the nine-time Mount Panorama conqueror's tragic death.

A long-time protege of Brock, seven-time Bathurst 1000 winner Lowndes will line up for his 33rd bid at claiming the holy grail of Australian motorsport.

Bathurst 1000: How to watch, race start time and weather forecast Here is what you need to know about this weekend's Bathurst 1000, including when the race begins and how you can follow the action.

The 52-year-old will share the number 15 Team 18 wildcard with Super2 racer Bayley Hall after Triple Eight Racing Engineering ditched Chevrolet for Ford last year.

Lowndes has paired with rookies since former Triple Eight teammate Jamie Whincup's retirement in 2021, a move that helps the three-time Supercars champion pass on Brock's legacy.

"I'm somewhat gone full circle," Lowndes said today.

"Bayley, we did a track walk the other day, and I literally recalled everything that Peter taught me; from Turn 1, from Hell Corner, all the way around to Murray's Corner.

"For me, I'm hopefully passing on that legacy in some way … it is a milestone year. There's no doubt about that."

Peter Brock, pictured in 2004, won the Bathurst 1000 a record nine times. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Ask Lowndes what he remembers of Brock's counsel, and he will condense his knowledge of the track's 23 corners into a minute: advice like doing all your braking over Skyline or looking for the kink on the inside of the Elbow for your turn-in point.

"Peter was more than just a teammate," Lowndes said.

"His legacy will live on forever. He was bigger than the sport in some regards.

"He was just very much a person that could capture people's attention, hold their attention, but also inspire them for greatness.

"Those are the parts that I miss 20 years on."

Just weeks after Brock died in 2006, Lowndes roared to an emotional Bathurst 1000 win with an up-and-coming Jamie Whincup to pay tribute to his great mate.

Just weeks after Peter Brock's death, Craig Lowndes (left) and Jamie Whincup won the Bathurst 1000 in 2006. (Getty Images: LAT Images/Mark Horsburgh)

"History shows that the gap at the end of the day was 0.5, and that was Brock's number for a long time," Lowndes said.

Whincup added: "The minute's silence, I'll never forget that."

"You generally got someone on the hill yell out or whatnot, but that day, even the birds stopped chirping.

"It was my first (Bathurst) win for the team and a memory that I'll take to the grave."

Seven-time champion Whincup won't be on the grid for the first time since his 2002 debut, making way for Nick Percat to link up with title contender Broc Feeney, and allowing him to focus on his duties as Triple Eight team principal.

Feeney and Percat will be smarting after a horror outing at last month's The Bend 500, finishing 24th out of 26 cars at the Bathurst 1000 curtain-raiser.

The Triple Eight star has never won the 1,000km epic and is second in the standings behind last year's race winner and Grove Racing star Matt Payne.

title: WA's oil and gas industry watches impact of High Court ruling closely
text:
A High Court ruling in New South Wales has Western Australia's energy industry "deeply concerned" about future investment in the resource-rich state.

The ruling stymied the planned expansion of MACH Energy's coal mine after it had already been approved by NSW planning authorities in 2022, after three out of five judges ruled in favour of a community group, Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMSHEG).

The ruling found the planning authorities were required to take into account the emissions caused by using the coal MACH would export, otherwise known as the project's scope 3 emissions.

While the ruling is an interpretation of NSW planning laws, the energy industry is concerned effects could be felt on the other side of the country.

In WA, Woodside's $30 billion Browse gas proposal, which would produce more than 11 million tonnes of gas per year, is still being considered by state and federal environmental bodies.

Industry concerned

Independent oil and gas consultant Jeanette Roberts said the decision affirmed industry fears of "lawfare".

"One of the issues that concerns the industry in general is this lawfare of an approval being given and then an opportunity for it to be challenged, and the approval rescinded," she said.

"International investors will come because they believe that there's certainty and a rule of law and understanding what the rules and ground rules are.

"That certainly swings the pendulum away from that."

Aaron Morey says the implications of the decision need to be taken seriously. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

Chamber of Minerals and Energy WA chief executive Aaron Morey said it was "deeply concerning".

"If we shoot ourselves in the foot and we don't allow the development of these sorts of projects, then what you'll find is that new projects will spring up in other countries with lower environmental controls and standards," Mr Morey said.

Mr Morey said it was important that everyone took the implications of the decision as seriously as possible.

"Those are the sorts of issues that we need to more deeply understand," he said.

The Conservation Council of WA executive director Matt Roberts said it was common sense for all the environmental and climate impacts of a project to be considered in the approvals process.

"Australia can't wash its hands of the emissions caused when coal, oil or gas that is extracted here ends up being burnt overseas," he said.

"Gas export projects like Woodside's Browse proposal at Scott Reef risk massive climate damage because of their scope 3 emissions.

"We've always said that state and federal governments need to consider these scope 3 emissions when assessing these projects."

Interstate impact possible

Johnson Legal director Elaine Johnson said while it was an interpretation of NSW laws, the decision would be relevant to courts in other jurisdictions.

"The High Court of Australia has issued its first climate ruling, so obviously the content of that decision is going to be relevant to other courts in different jurisdictions around the country, including, I would assume, Western Australia," Ms Johnson said.

Johnson Legal represented DAMSHEG, the NSW environmental group that won in the High Court.

Woodside's Perth headquarters. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

While Ms Johnson said the decision would cause ripples for WA, University of Melbourne lecturer Liz Hicks told the ABC the decision would primarily affect NSW.

"The decision turns on NSW law, so its direct effect on other states is limited, but courts and decision-makers across the country will take note."

Last September, Environment Minister Murray Watt granted Woodside an extension of its Burrup Peninsula facilities until 2070 and said the project's impact on climate change did not have to be considered, as most of the resource would be exported overseas.

Australia is one of the world's largest exporters of LNG, accounting for about a fifth of global LNG trade.

Premier confident not the end of Browse

WA Premier Roger Cook said the decision would not spell the end of the WA Browse gas project.

"No, Browse is undergoing the environmental approval process both under the state regime but also under the national regime as well," he said.

"There are very stringent regulations they have to pass through.

"Ultimately this was a decision the High Court made about a state jurisdiction in New South Wales and so we need to understand if there are any implications for WA and what they may be."

Roger Cook says the ruling does not spell the end of Woodside's Browse proposal. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

A Woodside spokesperson said the company was aware of the High Court decision and would review it.

Mr Cook said he needed to look more closely at the implication of the decision.

Federal Labor cabinet minister Anne Aly said while the Commonwealth did not have any involvement in the case, the court had made the right decision.

"We've always said that new projects need to stack up environmentally, they need to stack up economically," she said.

"In this case, the court has made a decision that this project does not stack up environmentally."

title: Art loan scheme on chopping block amid Tasmanian cost cutting
text:
Tasmania's arts sector is fearing for the future of a nation-leading purchasing scheme that looks to be affected by government job cuts.

The COLLECT Art Purchase Scheme offers no-interest loans of up to $8,000 to purchase Tasmanian-made artworks, which can be paid off over 12 months.

As part of a restructure of the department overseeing Arts Tasmania, 250 jobs are set to be lost, including several in the arts sector.

The ABC understands that this includes the role administering COLLECT and several more from the team handling grants programs.

Loading Instagram content

Painter Faridah Cameron urged the government to protect the program, Which she said was vital to her earning a living as a professional artist.

"You know, someone has to produce this stuff," she said.

"Artists are at the beginning of a surprisingly long economic chain, and it will be devastating to Tasmanian artists if the COLLECT scheme were lost."

Cameron said about 50 per cent of her paintings were sold through the scheme, often to people who may otherwise not have made the purchase.

"So, potentially, if the COLLECT scheme went down, that would represent about half of my income," she said.

Printmaker Mandy Renard said she too received about half her sales through the program.

"I got so much out of it as an artist," she said.

"I feel like the next generation that are coming up are going to have even more trouble getting into the system and working full time as artists."

Loading Instagram content

Nation 'jealous' of program

A spokesperson for Building Tasmania — formerly State Growth — told the ABC that "there has been no plan put forward to end the COLLECT program".

Handmark Gallery owner Allanah Dopson questioned how the scheme could continue if there was nobody left to organise it.

"It's sort of a no-brainer that this is something the government can actually do in the arts that isn't costing them any money," she said.

According to the COLLECT website, more than 6,700 artworks worth a combined $22 million have been sold through the program since 2009.

Along with art, it can also be used to purchase handmade furniture and jewellery.

A 1.5 per cent administration fee is also charged on sales, meaning much of the cost is recovered.

Emma Bett says the scheme is used by returning customers who "come back and buy another work". (ABC News: Andrew Cunningham)

Gallery co-director Emma Bett said the rest of the nation was "very jealous" of the COLLECT scheme, which was run only in Tasmania.

"It's the only state in the country to have it and to be forward-thinking enough to support our artists like this," she said.

"It's such a small, small outlay by the government to create this incredible program that is a stimulus.

"We also have returning customers who, because it takes a year to pay off a work, will take that year and then, once they've paid it off, come back and buy another work.

"It works really well for young collectors who otherwise wouldn't have bought or would have banged it on the credit card."

Loading Instagram content

Government 'doesn't value art sector': Greens

Greens Deputy Leader and Arts spokesperson Vica Bayley said it would be an "absolute travesty" if the COLLECT scheme ended.

"It has flow-on benefits for framers, for transporters, for others who are involved in the art scene, and it's been a raging success," she said.

"It's clear that this government doesn't value the art sector, despite the fact that it delivers a massive amount to our economy, to our community, to our sense of place, and to our place in the world."

Twenty minutes' notice of Tasmanian job cuts, union says Tasmanian public service workers have been left in tears after snap meetings where they were informed about job cuts in their teams, a union says.

The sector has also been left reeling by proposed staffing cuts at the Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery.

They include the head of the Tasmanian Herbarium, who is an internationally acclaimed lichen researcher, as well as librarian, graphic designer, photographer and senior exhibition officer roles.

It is not just jobs in the arts that are being slashed. State government departments have been told to find $1.5 billion in savings to help Treasurer Eric Abetz balance the budget.

Among the jobs set to go are some in the education department's Inclusive Practice Team, which works to support children with disabilities.

Eight days before those cuts were announced, Education Minister Jo Palmer's office told the ABC that "there has been no proposal put forward to reduce staff numbers".

title: Female rage inspires new adaptation of classic novel Little Women
text:
When Kathryn Marquet was 18, she wasn't interested in anything but making art.

"If anyone had told me at 18, 'You have to get married now', I'd have been like, 'What are you talking about?'" the Brisbane-based actor and playwright says.

"I had other stuff to do first."

Marquet is tapping into that feeling as she co-adapts Louisa May Alcott's Little Women for the stage for Queensland Theatre Company (QTC)'s 2027 season.

In Little Women, Jo March, the second-eldest of four sisters, yearns for a creative life while rejecting the constraints of her gender and the expectation of marriage.

It follows recent adaptations of other coming-of-age novels about young women, from the My Brilliant Career musical to A Room with a View.

These classic stories are finding audiences as young women today continue to grapple with ideas around feminism and choice: from trad wives to the myth of "having it all", she says.

"These characters have other passions, other obsessions and an inner world that exists far beyond the need of a husband," Marquet says.

"We're told we can have a job, children, this and this, but the reality is it's profoundly difficult."

The playwright is excited to explore these ideas through Jo, a character with whom she's always identified.

"Jo feels very out of place in the world she inhabits," Marquet says. "She struggles with her anger because she wants so much more than is being offered to her.

" I think a lot of young women have that experience and aren't sure where they fit in the world. "

Marquet sees Jo's fiery temper as resonating with today, when, she explains, "female rage isn't an acceptable sin".

"We're encouraged to be sweet and kind and together, so what do you do with your rage?"

A cozy world

On the flip side of rage, Marquet and her co-writer, fellow Brisbane playwright Maxine Mellor, have been grappling with the question of how to be a good person in a time of crisis, like Jo March.

QTC's 2027 season An Iliad by Homer; adapted by Lisa Peterson and Denis O'Hare

Romeo + Juliet by William Shakespeare; adapted by Isaac Drandic and Kamarra Bell-Wykes

Miss Fisher's Murder Mysteries: Death by Deckchair by Deb Cox

Stereophonic by David Adjmi

Counting and Cracking by S Shakthidharan

Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street by Stephen Sondheim (music and lyrics) and Hugh Wheeler (book)

My Roman Empire by Alberto Di Troia

Little Women by Louisa May Alcott; adapted by Kathryn Marquet and Maxine Mellor

In Little Women, she tries to figure out how to help as her father serves in the Union Army in the American Civil War. That also has parallels with today.

"All these terrible things are happening overseas and we want to help, but we don't quite know what to do," she says.

"The challenges of being a good person in a complex world are still as relevant today as they were when Louisa May Alcott first wrote Little Women."

While there are contemporary resonances to Little Women, part of the appeal for Marquet of adapting a book that is so well-known and loved is in offering a kind of balm to an audience.

"We want to create this beautiful, cozy world where people can go into the theatre and have a moment of escape and feel safe and feel all the good things about the human condition," she says.

For QTC artistic director Daniel Evans, commissioning a new Little Women was about getting together a group of artists he admires. Not just Marquet and Mellor, but Brisbane director Bridget Boyle and Brisbane actor and playwright Courtney Cavallaro, who will play Jo.

It reflects Evans's appreciation of the local independent scene in which he developed as a writer and director.

"I grew up and came of age surrounded by amazing women, particularly in the independent sector," he says.

" I'm only here because of them, so it's a bit of a gift or a love letter or acknowledgement of these incredible makers of enormous heart and enormous talent. "

Difficulties facing drama in Queensland

Little Women is one of two new adaptations by artists from Queensland in QTC's season, alongside a new Romeo + Juliet from First Nations theatre-makers Isaac Drandic and Kamarra Bell-Wykes.

Romeo + Juliet will be the story of how two lovers are divided by a broken songline in the earth. (Supplied: QTC)

The idea for an all-Indigenous Romeo + Juliet came from Drandic, the company's Head of First Nations Theatre.

Evans is excited to see a First Nations dramaturgical lens applied to one of the world's most famous plays.

"You can't understand through a Western European dramaturgical lens the way a First Nations culture experiences time, love, fraternity and connection," Evans explains.

"That wrestle is where the bravery and excitement of that project is for me."

Making space for local theatre-makers, like Marquet, Mellor and Drandic, is important to Evans.

"I'm constantly in dialogue with everyone, going, 'How do we put Queensland front and centre?'" he says.

"I spend a lot of my job advocating for Queensland and for Queensland artists, while trying to punch up into that national conversation as well."

He's heartened by the depth of talent and skill throughout the Queensland arts community, but aware of the constraints facing the industry.

An Iliad, starring Brisbane local David Wenham, transfers to Queensland Theatre Company in 2027. (Supplied: STC/Daniel Boud)

Evans points to the dwindling of theatre and technical production courses across the country, including Queensland University of Technology cutting the state's only degree in technical production.

It's one of 48 creative arts degrees across Australia that were discontinued between 2018 and 2025.

" Young school leavers being able to enter the industry, to study a technical trade or design course, is difficult," Evans says. "That's something that weighs on my mind. "

At the same time, across the country, enrolments in high school drama courses fell by 39 per cent in the eight years to 2023.

In Queensland, the number of schools offering drama fell by 22 per cent, from 323 to 253 between 2020 and 2025, with enrolments falling 39 per cent, from 3,576 in 2020 to 2,194 in 2025.

Those statistics emphasise the importance of QTC education programs such as The Scene Project, in which the company commissions a new short play that is then workshopped and performed by high school students from 130 schools across Queensland.

"Things like The Scene Project and our Young Company [an ensemble of performers in years 9 to 12] have to continue," Evans says.

"When things do tighten, those are the things we have to keep on the table, otherwise we're not going to have a future generation of makers."

Dreaming bigger

It's all part of the answer to the central question for Evans when planning QTC's 2027 season, his second since becoming artistic director: What does the industry need?

"Right now, we need to dream a bit bigger," he says.

"The best thing I can do for Queensland artists, technicians and audiences is just to punch and swing big."

Those big swings include the Brisbane premiere of An Iliad, starring David Wenham, after its sell-out season in Sydney this year; producing a musical, Sweeney Todd, at a time when some commercial theatre productions are cutting runs of major musicals short; and bringing S Shakthidharan's three-hour epic Counting and Cracking to Queensland for the first time.

Counting and Cracking will also have a free outdoor season in New York in 2027. (Supplied: Belvoir)

"The cast sizes are big, the worlds are really epic, and all the stories are quite high stakes, or the characters are at an emotional crucible," Evans says.

The season also includes a new Australian play, the just-announced winner of the $30,000 Queensland Premier's Drama Award: My Roman Empire by Alberto Di Troia.

It's the story of a queer man travelling to his ancestral home in rural Italy and finding it's not "the Eat Pray Love, La Dolce Vita [he] thought it would be". Instead, his long-lost family are neo-fascists.

Sandro Colarelli and Will Bartolo will star in My Roman Empire at QTC. (Supplied: QTC)

Evans's sense of ambition also extends to co-productions with other companies: Stereophonic with Melbourne Theatre Company and Belvoir St Theatre in Sydney; and Miss Fisher's Murder Mysteries: Death by Deckchair with Sydney Theatre Company. Evans will direct both.

"These big works we're all staging together [like Stereophonic] are our way of going: 'We want to bring the best theatre in the world to you,'" he says.

At the same time, those collaborations meet Evans's aim of creating pathways for local artists.

"We get to send and showcase some of our amazing Queensland actors and creators to southern states, and that's worth a lot," he says.

title: Woman loses medical negligence claim over partially amputated leg
text:
A woman who alleged doctors unnecessarily amputated her lower left leg has lost her medical negligence claim against the Hunter New England Local Health District (HNELHD).

During a two-week Supreme Court civil hearing in May, Vesna Zvicer alleged medical negligence, claiming psychological and physical injury.

She was admitted to John Hunter Hospital in Newcastle on November 11, 2020 and amputation was recommended when her condition — sepsis — worsened.

The procedure was carried out in January 2021 at Macquarie University Hospital but Ms Zvicer argued her leg was "salvageable" and sought damages on behalf of herself and her children.

On Wednesday New South Wales Supreme Court Justice Edward Muston dismissed her claim.

"I have concluded that HNELHD did not breach the duty of care it owed to Ms Zvicer," he said.

"For the same reasons as I have given in reaching that conclusion, I am not satisfied that HNELHD breached any duty of care it owed to Ms Zvicer’s children."

Sepsis and necrosis in left leg

The court heard Ms Zvicer had extreme generalised sepsis and acute compartment syndrome in her lower left leg.

The court heard surgeons "prodded and poked" the leg muscle and determined the leg was dead and unviable. They feared Ms Zvicer's heel could become gangrenous.

Vesna Zvicer's lawyers argued doctors could not have been certain her leg was necrotic without fasciotomy surgery. (Supplied: Vesna Zvicer)

But Ms Zvicer's barrister Adam Casselden SC said doctors could not have been certain her leg was necrotic without performing a fasciotomy.

"Just looking at the skin and poking it doesn't answer the question [of] is this necrotic and how severe it is," Mr Casselden said.

He said the procedure should have been done, opening the muscle up and relieved compartment pressure.

Fasciotomies were performed on Ms Zvicer's right leg and left and right thighs, but not her left leg.

Justice Muston said clinicians weighed the risks when deciding to proceed with amputation.

"The chance, if any, of salvaging Ms Zvicer’s left leg had to be weighed against the risks associated with performing a fasciotomy on that limb," he said.

"The first of those risks lay in the fact that Ms Zvicer was critically unwell when the surgery was performed."

The case was heard in the Supreme Court in Sydney. (ABC News: Jamie McKinnell)

Ms Zvicer's legal team told the court Ms Zvicer was well enough to undergo fasciotomy surgery, but it was ruled out.

Fear of death without amputation

The court heard when the amputation was scheduled in January 2021, she discharged herself from John Hunter Hospital only to return after becoming unwell.

Ms Zvicer was ultimately transferred to Macquarie University Hospital, where the amputation was carried out on January 16, 2021.

HNELHD argued the operating surgeon "acted in a manner which, at the time, would have been widely accepted in Australia by peer professional opinion as competent professional practice".

Justice Muston ultimately accepted the surgeon's fears she could die without an amputation.

"The tissue breakdown associated with muscle death causes the release of chemicals from within the cells that make up that tissue," he said.

"If pressure in a dead compartment was released — these chemicals wash out into the patient’s bloodstream and can cause major cardiovascular collapse and, potentially, death."

Ms Zvicer's legal team was steadfast in their belief the lower left leg was not dead.

Justice Muston dismissed Ms Zvicer's claim and claims on behalf of her children and ordered her to pay the health service's costs.

title: NZ Rugby launches court bid to protect 'Chiefs' name from PNG league franchise
text:
Rugby union officials have launched New Zealand High Court proceedings to prevent the National Rugby League's (NRL) new Papua New Guinea-based franchise from using the "Chiefs" name in New Zealand.

New Zealand Rugby (NZR) said the move was an effort to protect the brand of the Waikato-based Chiefs, who have played in the Super Rugby competition across Australasia since rugby union turned professional in 1996.

The NRL, which is Australia-based but has one team in the New Zealand city of Auckland, announced the expansion of the league to Papua New Guinea in 2024.

The island nation's Prime Minister James Marape unveiled the name "Chiefs" the following year.

James Marape (front, second from right) announced the PNG Chiefs' name in October 2025. (Supplied: NRL)

NZR said attempts to engage the Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC) over the issue had been unsuccessful and it was seeking an interim and final injunction against the use of the name before the Papua New Guinea team was officially launched later this month.

"For 30 years the Chiefs and their players have built an incredibly strong identity that is widely recognised and loved by fans," NZR chief executive Steve Lancaster said in a statement today.

"We have raised our concerns with the ARLC directly and consistently over the last year in attempting to find a resolution. We now have a responsibility to protect the Chiefs brand."

Action branded 'hypocritical'

ARLC executive chairman Peter V'landys said the complaint was hypocritical given the New South Wales rugby league team had used the "Blues" brand for more than half a century before the Auckland Blues Super Rugby franchise was launched 30 years ago.

"We will defend this vigorously," he said.

"The hypocrisy is mind-blowing, considering the Auckland Blues in 1996 used the NSW Blues name without any consultation or approval.

"Rugby union is obviously feeling threatened by rugby league in New Zealand, with sell-outs at most rugby league games."

Rugby league split from rugby union in the late 19th century in a dispute about amateurism.

PNG Chiefs face 'danger of brand confusion' over team name Australia's intellectual property agency tells PNG's rugby league franchise that its chosen name, the Chiefs, risks being confused with the name of a Super Rugby club.

While union is the more popular game globally, league rules the roost on Australia's eastern seaboard and has been making great strides in New Zealand.

Papua New Guinea is the only country in the world where rugby league is the most popular sport.

The new team has already signed a slew of top NRL players ahead of its first season in 2028, and will be backed by hundreds of millions of dollars in funding from the Australian government, which is looking to shore up its influence in the Pacific Islands.

"We want to be absolutely clear, this is not about rugby league's growth in the Pacific," Mr Lancaster said.

"We welcome the development of the Pacific region through sport and the passion that the people of Papua New Guinea have for both rugby and rugby league."

The ABC has contacted PNG Chiefs CEO Lorna McPherson, IP Australia and Mr Lancaster for comment.

title: Major share market float of Firmus in trouble as interest wanes
text:
It was touted as the biggest float since Telstra in the 1990s, but the share market float of data centre operator Firmus is in trouble before it has even hit the share market.

The bookbuild for the float closed today.

That is, investment banks have stopped taking bids for the initial public offering (IPO) and will now determine at what price the company lists on the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX).

Firmus was set to hit the boards of the ASX at $11 per share, but reports suggest that price may have been set too high.

Market participants have been underwhelmed by the float's roadshow, with some criticising it for having an "unprecedented lack of detail" and others concerned about its debt and energy needs.

The float, or total number of shares on issue, is reportedly having to be revalued down because of the lacklustre interest, with reports it could drop to about $8 per share.

Late Wednesday, the company's representatives also pulled out of an appearance before a parliamentary inquiry into artificial intelligence today, with reports the troubled IPO was the reason for the no-show.

Is Firmus here for a good time or a long time? Data Centre operator about to float on Australian share market.

Mounting concerns from investors

Firmus is a so-called neocloud technology company.

It builds, owns and operates upscale data centres or so-called "AI factories", used to run and train artificial intelligence models.

The firm is raising cash from investors to build an AI factory in Launceston and plans for two more in Tasmania.

But its ambitions extend across Australia and into South-East Asian markets as well.

Reports suggest Firmus intends to raise up to $7 billion from institutional and retail investors in its IPO, which could value the company at more than $50 billion.

But the conclusion of a $73 billion partnership with data centre firm CDC and community backlash for proposed suburban data centres has caused concern for investors.

Firmus co-founder Oliver Curtis was also jailed for 12 months in 2016 for a 2007 insider trading scheme.

Portfolio manager 'steering clear'

Ten Cap portfolio manager Jun Bei Liu said she was steering clear of the Firmus IPO, concerned about what she said was an "unprecedented lack of detail" being disclosed and enormous structural risks.

"Firmus is probably one of the most polarising IPOs I have ever seen," she observed.

" I think Firmus is a very high-risk proposition — very high profile, but with enormous risk involved. "

She said 97 per cent of the data centre capacity they had promised had not been built.

"They might deliver cheaper earnings in two years if they build what they promise, but that's speculative," she said.

Ten Cap's Jun Bei Liu says she won't be taking up the Firmus IPO. (ABC News: John Gunn)

"We much prefer to be in the companies that actually build those data centres — the engineers, the electrical contractors.

" There are a lot of those smaller businesses now benefiting from the huge build-out that Australia is about to see. "

Caution over Firmus 'euphoria'

Morningstar senior market strategist Lochlan Halloway said he saw "the hallmarks of the boom phase … if not outright euphoria" because of Firmus's wild increase in valuation in such a short period of time.

The company's valuation surged from about $6.9 billion in April and was now at $15.5 billion.

"Not bad for a start-up," he said.

Mr Halloway was particularly concerned with the company's debt.

"The neoclouds are heavily geared. The model is to borrow against customer contracts to buy chips, then use the rent to repay the loans," he said in an economic note.

Lochlan Halloway says he's not written Firmus off entirely. (ABC News)

Once its data centres are built, Firmus expects to be carrying about US$30 billion of debt, around six times the US$5 billion of operating earnings it forecasts for 2028.

"Borrowed money alone does not make a bubble, and plenty of infrastructure is sensibly funded with debt. But credit is the common thread running through essentially every boom and bust cycle," he wrote.

But he did not write the company off completely.

"For investors, what matters is how that fair value compares to the float price," Mr Halloway said.

'Ambitious' data centres plans need major local power upgrades

Accela Research published one of the first comprehensive reports on data centres in January this year.

Its lead data centre analyst Naomi Wagura described the company has having "ambitious growth plans" that could "significantly reshape electricity infrastructure" in areas where its data centres would locate.

AI data centre provider could become one of Australia's biggest stock floats AI data centre developer Firmus Technologies is seeking investors ahead of a multi-billion-dollar share market float next month.

In Tasmania, Firmus's three planned data centres would make it the state's largest energy consumer, needing some 444 megawatts if they went ahead, and would crucially require the island state to add extra generation.

"This infrastructure investment needs binding customer commitments and realistic demand forecasts, with clear arrangements for who pays if demand arrives late or falls short," Ms Wagura said.

And while there were clear potential benefits to locals, she cautioned there also needed to be "clear disclosure and enforceable obligations".

The company is scheduled to float on the ASX on October 23.

title: Wallabies resist urge to shift Suaalii from wing for Bledisloe Cup Test
text:
The Wallabies have kept Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii on the wing for Saturday night's Bledisloe Cup Test at Auckland's Eden Park, with Isaac Henry named in the centres.

Henry has been included at outside centre to partner Len Ikitau in the Wallabies' midfield against the All Blacks.

Ikitau, who has recovered from an ankle injury, moves from outside to inside centre in the wake of Hunter Paisami's suspension.

Wallabies upset Boks in Perth The Wallabies manage to overcome four late yellow cards to defeat world champions South Africa 42-38 in a pulsating Test in Perth.

Wallabies coach Les Kiss resisted the temptation to shift Suaalii from the wing back to the centres.

He has shown faith in 27-year-old Henry, who he coached at the Queensland Reds.

Kiss also handed Henry his Test debut two months ago, against Japan in Osaka.

Henry, who will be playing his fifth Test, is the only change to the Wallabies' starting XV following their stunning 42-38 win over world champions South Africa in Perth late last month.

The Wallabies made four changes on the reserves bench, opting for a 5-3 (forwards-back split).

Hooker Josh Nasser, prop Massimo De Lutiis, back-rower Nick Champion de Crespigny and fly half Declan Meredith earned call-ups.

De Lutiis and Champion de Crespigny are the respective replacements for Taniela Tupou and Tom Hooper, who have returned to their European clubs.

Isaac Henry will wear the number 13 jersey against the All Blacks. (Getty Images: Paul Miller)

"Keeping consistency in the starting side gives us a solid foundation, while adding some freshness on the bench will provide energy late in the game," Kiss said in a statement.

The Wallabies have enjoyed a six-match unbeaten streak after beginning the Test season with defeats to Ireland and France in the Nations Championship.

Since Kiss took over from Joe Schmidt as coach, the Wallabies have recorded four wins and a draw.

But the All Blacks pose an almighty challenge, especially at Eden Park.

The Wallabies have lost 24 consecutive Tests against the All Blacks at the venue, with their most recent victory coming in 1986.

They did, however, beat Wales at Eden Park in the third-place play-off at the 2011 Rugby World Cup.

"There aren't many tougher challenges than playing New Zealand at Eden Park, but it's one we're excited by and know that we will need to be at our best in all aspects of our game," Kiss said.

Damian McKenzie will start at fly half for the All Blacks. (Getty Images: Fiona Goodall)

Meanwhile, injury has forced the All Blacks to name Damian McKenzie at fly half as they look to maintain their stranglehold on the Bledisloe Cup.

McKenzie will start at 10 after Ruben Love (ankle) and Richie Mo'unga (calf) were ruled out.

Beauden Barrett will play fullback, with McKenzie having held down the role for all four Tests in the All Blacks' recent 3-1 series loss to the Springboks.

All three Barrett brothers will start against the Wallabies, with ex-captain Scott named at lock and Jordie slotting in the backline at inside centre.

The All Blacks have held the Bledisloe Cup since 2003.

title: Government under pressure to intervene over ATO credit card ban
text:
The federal government is facing growing pressure over the Australian Taxation Office's (ATO) decision to stop accepting credit card payments for tax bills, with small business groups and crossbench MPs warning the move could make it harder for businesses to manage cash flow.

Labor frontbenchers have presented a confusing picture of the government's position, with some urging the tax office to resume discussions with the business sector, while Assistant Technology Minister Andrew Charlton has said the government backs the ATO.

Housing Minister Clare O'Neil defended the Reserve Bank's decision to scrap the credit card fees, but indicated the government was worried about the ATO's response and the impact on small businesses.

"The government does have some real concerns about what the ATO is proposing to do here," Ms O'Neil said on Thursday.

"We really want the ATO to go back and talk to business about what they have decided to do here and think about how they can find a solution that works for everyone."

Small Business Minister Anne Aly yesterday urged the ATO to "keep talking with small businesses" and "find a way forward".

"I've spoken to small businesses and they were rightly shocked by this decision, and I do think they should have been consulted," she said.

Andrew Charlton says businesses would be able to find a workaround. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

But Mr Charlton said small businesses that had previously relied on credit cards to pay tax bills would be able to find a workaround, pointing to flexible repayment schedules already available through the taxation office.

"The government supports the ATO's decision," he said.

"If we're saying that surcharges can't exist in the private sector, then surcharges shouldn't exist in the public sector."

Business groups call for government intervention

The ATO met with small business groups on September 30 to foreshadow the public announcement the following day.

ATO will not budge on credit card ban after meeting with business groups Small business groups say the ATO has indicated it will not reverse its decision to stop accepting credit card payments.

Business groups were then invited to a meeting yesterday "to answer follow-up questions and work through implementation and transitional arrangements for affected taxpayers".

The tax office ban on credit card use will start on December 1.

"The ATO will continue to engage with stakeholders, supporting taxpayers and tax practitioners, and seek opportunities to promote awareness through consistent communication and key messages," an ATO spokesperson said.

Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive Andrew McKellar said there should be a "clear message from government" in support of small business.

"It's now time, I think, for the political leadership in government to stand up and really say to the tax office, 'This is not how it works,'" Mr McKellar said.

"Hopefully by the end of today or certainly by the end of the week … the tax office will be listening."

Members of the crossbench have also raised concerns about the change, with independent Kate Chaney calling on the ATO to reconsider the ban or grant businesses a longer grace period to adjust.

"Times are tough for small business owners," she said.

Kate Chaney says the ATO should reconsider the ban. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

"Credit cards are one way businesses manage cashflow when a tax bill lands. Removing that option with around eight weeks' notice makes things harder."

Community Strong Australia MP Allegra Spender said the government must work with the ATO to find a "workable solution".

"Managing cash flow is difficult at the best of times and businesses need to have the flexibility offered by credit," she said.

Government tries to tap into public frustration

The change was announced after the Reserve Bank of Australia, which is independent, banned credit card surcharges across the board, a move hailed by Labor as a cost-of-living win for taxpayers.

Last week, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Attorney-General Michelle Rowland posted videos to social media celebrating the change, which Mr Albanese said would save Australians money "every time you tap".

But public sentiment has swiftly turned since cafes and other small businesses simply increased prices for consumers in a bid to recoup fees still owed to the banks.

Government accused of 'staggering double standard' as ATO bans credit card payments Surcharge bans are supposed to save consumers money but retailers say they're being forced to put prices up and are finding ways around the reforms.

Mr Charlton today rejected concerns that ending surcharges would force businesses to lift prices, saying payment processing costs had fallen.

"That reduction means that card payments are cheaper for businesses to process, so there's no reason as a result of this reform that consumers should be paying more when they tap their card for a coffee," he said.

The Coalition had slammed the credit card surcharge ban as a farce, with Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie saying ending the surcharge would not make everyday items cheaper.

"The prime minister promised that removing the surcharge would make coffees go down," she said.

"Guess what? It doesn't disappear. Businesses are being expected to absorb it."

Independent member for Fowler Dai Le said the government had failed to "read the room" and said small businesses were already under strain due to rising fuel and energy costs, but did not want to raise prices for consumers.

"This is one more blow to the ever-increasing costs of running their own business and they don't know if they can keep their doors open into the future," she said.

Business leaders have demanded the government clarify its stance on the Australian Taxation Office’s sudden removal of credit cards as a payment method, after Labor ministers contradicted each other over the move. The tax office surprised small business owners earlier this month as the Reserve Bank of Australia’s ban on credit card surcharges came into effect. The ATO said it would stop taking credit card payments for tax bills from November 30, arguing it could not absorb the fees. Housing Minister Clare O’Neil said the government had concern’s over the ATO’s proposal. Alex Ellinghausen The ban, which Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has spruiked as a cost-of-living measure that would save households $1.6 billion a year, has incurred the wrath of small businesses and the opposition. Small Business Minister Anne Aly was the first to raise concerns over the ATO’s move on Wednesday, urging the tax office to consult more widely about the ban’s implementation. Cabinet minister Clare O’Neil weighed in on Thursday morning, saying the government had “some real concerns about what the ATO is proposing to do here”.

Advertisement

“Small businesses across the country really struggle to manage their cash flow, and I know that partly because I grew up in a household where both my mum and my dad ran their own small business,” O’Neil told Nine’s Today show. The comments put her at odds with Assistant Minister for the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton, who shortly afterwards said the government “supports the ATO’s decision” and that the tax office was ensuring consistency between the public and private sectors. Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton said there was “no reason” for businesses to raise prices because of the surcharge ban. Alex Ellinghausen “They don’t want the people who are not paying by credit card, which is 98 per cent of taxpayers, to be subsidising those that do,” Charlton told ABC radio. The confusion sparked calls from the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry for the government to show leadership and provide businesses with certainty.

Advertisement

“We want a response, and we want one clear outcome which is consistent across government,” chief executive Andrew McKellar told reporters in Canberra. “We don’t want to see agencies like the tax office going alone and acting in this way.” McKellar said while the tax office has argued the change would only affect 5 per cent of businesses, that figure represented a quarter of a million small businesses. Loading The ATO stood by its decision after meeting with stakeholders on Wednesday, in a consultation that McKellar said was fruitless.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said on Thursday that Labor was “all over the shop”. Related Article Payments ‘Quite ill-prepared’: Shops scramble to meet new card surcharge ban “We’ve had the housing minister in one place, the small business minister somewhere else, and the de facto treasurer has been defending the ATO,” Taylor said. “But they should, from today, get rid of the ban, axe the ban that they’ve put on the ability of small businesses to pay tax with their credit cards.” Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson accused the government of double standards.

“The government says to small business, you’ve got to absorb these costs, but when it comes to payment systems to us, we’re not going to absorb those costs,” he told News24. In her Thursday morning interview, O’Neil backed the Reserve Bank’s call to scrap credit card fees, saying Labor’s position was that Australians should not be charged to spend their money. title: ‘Poets get rejected more’: The publishing lesson learnt by Lessons in Chemistry author Bonnie Garmus
text:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

American author Bonnie Garmus was on the cusp of 65 when her debut novel, Lessons in Chemistry, was published – after a career in copywriting and advertising, and an astonishing 98 rejections from agents for an earlier manuscript. The story of Elizabeth Zott, a brilliant chemist who becomes the unlikely star of a TV cooking show in 1960s California, went on to become a global sensation, selling almost 10 million copies and inspiring a hit TV series starring Brie Larson. Now Garmus is back with Peck & Peck, a funny, warm-hearted romp about Batter Gray, a poetry-obsessed recent graduate who lands a job at a prestigious poetry journal in 1980s New York. For all its whimsy, the novel has plenty to say about distinctly contemporary concerns: the battle between art and commerce, the value we place on art and artists, and what happens when culture becomes a business. We spoke to Garmus about obsessions, sudden fame and why poetry might just save the world. Your characters tend to be obsessives, whether that’s about rowing, chemistry, poetry or typography. What’s taking up an unreasonable amount of brain space for you at the moment? That’s a really good question. Right now we’re about six weeks away from publication, so I’m writing a lot of articles for different magazines and things, and that’s taking up a lot of headspace. But I’m also dedicated to reading one poem a day. I’ve been doing that since 2009, and I find that evens me out. Related Article Dicey Topics

Good Weekend Sexism at work made Bonnie Garmus start writing. It sold 7 million copies What started the project of reading one poem a day? When I was in high school, about 14 or 15, I had a really good English teacher, and every day, he would read a poem out loud. It was one of the things that we loved about his class. He made us promise at the end of the school year that we would read a poem a day for the rest of our lives. He said, “It’s not because I think that you need to study this person or this form; it’s because poetry will end up saving your life. It will keep your brain fresh, it will keep your ideas open, and you will explore the world through poetry.” So we all kept the promise for at least four hours – until the school year was over – and then I never read a poem. Then one day I was driving home from work, and I heard a poem by Nikki Giovanni on the radio. It was a poem my teacher had read, and it brought tears to my eyes. I thought, “Why hadn’t I kept this promise?” I felt like my brain was starting to rot and work was overwhelming, so on that day, I decided to fulfil that promise to him and started reading a poem a day. I know it sounds kind of ridiculous, but it actually matters so much. If you don’t have time to read an entire book or a long magazine article, you have time to read a poem. It’s so complex that it will actually help you in lots of ways you don’t really realise until you start getting into it, including upping your empathy and connecting you with your heartbeat a little more often. Poetry is at the heart of your delightful second novel, Peck & Peck. Was it this routine that provided the inspiration for the book? Really, it was my unhappiness at that time with technology. This is way back, before Lessons in Chemistry. I was having a reckoning with my career and it felt like technology was moving in the wrong direction.

Advertisement

When I first started writing in the technology space for advertising, it was so interesting, innovative and full of promise. Then it seemed to be slowly sliding into something that I didn’t recognise. It was becoming more about making money instead of making what was worthwhile. I was really at a crossroads with what I was doing, and I was turning down more and more work because I didn’t feel good about what they were doing. This was way back before people talked about AI all the time and what a danger it is, but back then, we all knew about it and knew it was a danger. It was simply that people took it more seriously than they do today, and they would have never allowed it to come out as unregulated as it has. Peck & Peck follows a devoted young poet, Batter Gray, who gets a job at a prestigious, if dysfunctional, poetry journal – the titular Peck & Peck – in New York in 1983. What part of the story came to you first? It was the Peck & Peck office building. As I walk around cities – I live in England – I think more and more we see the same thing over and over. We see another Kentucky Fried Chicken, another Starbucks, or whatever. There’s this creeping conformity that’s been going on for a long time around the world where we go for the familiar, and I wanted to create a building that was unfamiliar. It’s not like [Barcelona’s] Sagrada Família, but it’s like that in the sense that there’s only one in the world. At the heart of the novel is a battle between commercial imperative and artistic integrity. Do you think those two things can ever happily coexist? I think they’ve always been at each other’s throats, but the world has become much more devoted to technology in a way that worries me. Now technology has decided that it’s going to take over the arts and do the arts for us as well. I don’t want it to do the arts for us. Technology is not an artist, and it doesn’t have the ability to do it in the same way. So I do worry a lot that this idea that technology can do everything is really misguided. There’s always been a belief – and my character believes it – that you’re supposed to get a good job as a lawyer, in accounting, or somewhere where you can make a living, and I certainly understand that [laughs]. I have two kids, and if one of them had come home and said, “I’ve decided to become a poet for my living,” I would have said, “Oh, how interesting ... but you have to do something else as well.” So yeah, there’s always this push-pull. But it turns out the arts are every bit as vital as anything else – as medicine, lawyerly work, maths or science. They’re all vital. There is something incredibly touching about your character Batter Gray’s obsession with poetry. Many of the staff who work at Peck & Peck are also obsessed. Do you think we need more people who care unreasonably deeply about the arts? Is that the antidote to the role of technology now? Yeah, I think so. It occurred to me as I was writing this book that it would be just bizarre if poetry was the one thing that ended up saving us. Poetry – the least-admired, least-read art – stepping forward and saying, “Here’s what we need to do.” The strange thing about poetry is that it’s incredibly honest, and right now we live in a very dishonest age. Before you published Lessons in Chemistry – which has gone on to become a phenomenal bestseller, with millions of copies sold worldwide and a hit TV series – you worked across all kinds of different writing. Was novel-writing always the calling? Oh, I was always doing it. You know how in Hollywood, every star has a script in their drawer? In copywriting and advertising, every copywriter and creative director has a book in their drawer. It’s not that you don’t want to do it; it’s that it doesn’t pay. You can’t survive. Ninety-nine per cent of all writers don’t make more than minimum wage.

Advertisement

I was very lucky to have a bestseller – let’s face it, we’re almost up to 10 million copies around the world now – and I am extremely lucky to have hit this. But does it happen very often? No, it doesn’t. People think I’m crazy, but I still work outside of novels. I know a Pulitzer Prize winner who still holds a full-time job because you cannot depend on this job for your security. Before Lessons in Chemistry was published, is it right that you had written a big, epic novel that attracted quite a number of rejection letters? Ninety-eight, yeah! I was going for the world record, but according to poets, 98 is amateur hour. Poets get rejected much more than that (laughs). But yeah, I kept submitting this thing, and it was a behemoth. It was 700 pages long. I hadn’t done my research, because if I had, I would have known that nobody in the world wants to publish a 700-page novel by an unknown writer. I found that out the hard way, and once I learnt that important lesson, I went shorter and wrote a completely different book. Related Article Streaming Breakout bestseller Lessons in Chemistry was destined for a Hollywood makeover Lessons in Chemistry follows the character Elizabeth Zott, who leaves her career as a chemist and starts a cooking show. At what point did you realise that this novel had become something much bigger than maybe you ever imagined? I’m embarrassed to say that it took a couple of years for me to really understand how big Lessons in Chemistry had become. Even when I had a movie deal and a series deal, it still didn’t feel real. Then it very slowly unfolded. However, it’s not like I’m recognised in public; it’s not that kind of fame. It’s just that the book did a lot better than I thought it was going to do. Did that level of success change your relationship with writing at all? No, uh-uh. I still write everything the same way as if I were working on an assignment for work, and that really works for me. It’s not so much that I need the structure of a working day, but I know that there are going to be days of failure. I know there will be days when I just don’t write well or can’t think of exactly what I want to say, and that’s OK. I will just wait, be patient, and wait for that voice to come back. For me, no, it hasn’t changed at all. We started this conversation talking about obsession. To see us out, do you know what obsession is coming next for you? I do, but I can’t tell you about it because it may change into another obsession of mine. I love to write about things that I’m passionate about, and it turns out that I’m passionate about a lot of things. Right now, I’m very passionate about poetry having a real place in our society, but more to the point, that AI is wrong for us right now and isn’t doing the job. It’s scary. People always ask, “How do you get your ideas?” I don’t know – I have too many, and I guess I’m mad about a lot of things, so they just keep cropping up! This is an edited extract from a longer conversation on Good Weekend Talks.

title: 'Exposed for the sham it is': Celebrations as High Court blocks major coal mine expansion
text:
IN BRIEF: The High Court has ruled against a major coal mine expansion in NSW.

Campaigners have welcomed the first case to consider broad environmental impacts.

Australia's highest court has upheld a first-of-its-kind environmental challenge to overturn a major coal mine expansion, after a years-long community campaign in east-central NSW.

In a landmark decision on Wednesday, the High Court ruled against the proposed expansion of the Mount Pleasant coal mine near Muswellbrook, in the Upper Hunter region of NSW.

It is the first time a court has upheld that project approvals must account for the broad environmental impacts of burning fossil fuels.

Environmental campaigners have termed the decision a victory for all Australians and called on the government to move away from fossil fuels.

Australian resource company MACH Energy sought to extend the life of Mount Pleasant coal mine in NSW by 22 years — to 2048 — and nearly double its yearly output to 22 million tonnes of carbon dioxide per year.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The state planning commission approved the proposal in 2022 before local Hunter Valley residents launched a legal challenge.

While the first bid to block the expansion was dismissed, in 2025, the NSW Court of Appeal unanimously ruled the approval unlawful, after it found planning authorities are legally required to consider the climate impact of Scope 3 emissions on local communities.

Scope 3 emissions are classified as indirect emissions tied to a company's broader business activities by the Greenhouse Gas Protocol, the top international standard for measuring greenhouse gas emissions.

MACH Energy took the finding to the High Court, which struck down the appeal on Wednesday morning.

The company said while it was "disappointed" with the outcome, it accepts the court's decision and "will carefully review the judgment to understand its implications for future project assessments and environmental approvals."

Mining approvals for the coal mine were due to end in November, before an August approval offered a lifeline from the state government, allowing for a continuation of operations to the end of 2032, as well as an increase in the approved extraction rate from 10.5 to 12.5 million tonnes of coal per year.

A years-long fight

The original case was brought by Wendy Wales, a retired science teacher and the president of the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMSHEG).

On Wednesday, she said the ruling acknowledged the risks to Australians posed by climate-influencing activities.

"This ruling acknowledges that many Australian communities have already suffered extreme weather devastation," she said.

"Now the true and complete long-term costs of export coal on Australians, via the climate impact from burning that coal, must be considered."

DAMSHEG said the proposed coal mine extension would generate 870 million tonnes of carbon dioxide, 98 per cent of it from coal burned overseas.

Greens spokesperson for climate change and planning Sue Higginson said the court had "exposed the New South Wales coal approval process for the sham it is, and declared that new coal cannot be approved when 98 per cent of the climate pollution are ignored".

"The High Court have sided with the climate science and declared that the NSW Independent Planning Commission was wrong to ignore downstream emissions when approving a massive new coal project."

A legal precedent in NSW

The High Court upheld the refusal of the planning commission's Mount Pleasant plan approval because the scope 3 emissions were not properly assessed.

"By majority, the High Court held the (planning) commission had failed to consider imposing conditions to minimise to the greatest extent practicable all greenhouse gas emissions, specifically 'scope three' emissions as required (by law)," the court said in a summary.

Head of climate and energy at Greenpeace Australia Pacific, Joe Rafalowicz, called on the Australian government, as well as leaders at COP31, to find the "courage, leadership and grit" to move away from fossil fuels, adding that the ruling clearly set a binding precedent for environmental challenges in the state.

"It is legally imperative that all of the pollution from fossil fuel projects be considered before approving a new project."

Rafalowicz said it was a victory for Australians "bearing the brunt" of extreme weather fuelled by fossil fuel corporations.

"Coal and gas companies have claimed they are not responsible for their pollution because it happens overseas, but today Australia’s highest court sided with common sense and scientific evidence to find that every new coal and gas approval in this country could put us at risk, no matter where it is sold or burnt."

READ MORE The two-metre question that could wipe out a population

The Minerals Council of Australia said the decision was a "further blow" to Australia's prospects of meeting continued demand from global customers for our "high-quality coal".

"Developing a coal mine in Australia is already difficult enough because of long approval times, lawfare by activists and high royalties and other taxes," Minerals Council of Australia chief executive officer Tania Constable said in a statement.

"The decision sends a very negative signal to Australia’s trade and investment partners about sovereign risk in this market."

The council said resource companies should not be "forced into a situation where well-funded legal attacks over a number of years require a High Court appeal", adding that legal challenges "seek to game the legal system by creating uncertainty and delay without ever having to pay costs".

"Investors in Australia’s resource sector will carefully review the outcome from today’s High Court judgement."

title: 'I want to be here the rest of my life': Lionel Messi's emotional international retirement
text:
In brief Footballer Lionel Messi has played his final international match, scoring in a 3-0 win over Benin.

Messi announced he would retire from international matches following Argentina's World Cup final loss to Spain.

Lionel Messi brought the curtain down on his 21-year international career on Wednesday, bidding farewell to adoring Argentina fans in an emotional final appearance for the former world champions in Buenos Aires.

In a perfectly scripted finale, the 39-year-old widely regarded as the greatest football player in history signed off with his 126th international goal in front of 85,000 supporters as Argentina cruised to a 3-0 victory over Benin.

Messi, playing in his record-extending 208th international, also provided the assist for the opening goal scored by veteran Nicolas Otamendi, with Nico Paz also scoring.

But the match was a footnote to the occasion itself, which saw Messi savouring the adulation of the Monumental Stadium crowd one last time for an event which had been billed as 'The Last Tango'.

"It was a huge source of pride for me to defend this jersey for more than 20 years," Messi told fans in a post-match address.
