"Not coming anymore is going to be deeply painful. I swear I'd like to play for the rest of my life, because playing for the Argentina national team is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you."

Messi, though, said he had no regrets about his decision to retire, citing Argentina's gruelling World Cup campaign, which took place as his late father was seriously ill, as a factor.

"Even though I want to be here all my life, I feel that this is the moment. The last World Cup was too much, everything I had to live through," said Messi.

Beforehand, Messi wiped away tears as the bus carrying him and his Argentina teammates made its way through crowds of well-wishers en route to the stadium.

Messi took the field alongside his three children and received affectionate waves from his wife, Antonela Roccuzzo, and his mother, Celia Cuccittini, who were watching from a VIP box.

Shortly before kick-off, a giant Argentina jersey bearing the word "Gracias" (Thank You) above the football superstar's No.10 was laid out on the pitch as the crowd roared their approval.

Messi welled up again as Falklands War veteran Fabio Santana sang the national anthem beside a banner which read "The Malvinas are Argentine", the same banner held aloft by players after their 2-1 World Cup semi-final win over England.

The match was halted in the 10th minute — a tribute to Messi's famous shirt number — for a minute-long ovation to the former Barcelona and Paris Saint-Germain star.

He crowned the occasion with a goal from the penalty spot in the 71st minute.

'Gave it my all'

At the final whistle, a drone show lit up the night sky above the stadium, showing Messi's image and thanking the eight-time Ballon d'Or winner for his career.

Messi's farewell came two and a half months after Argentina's World Cup final defeat to Spain in New Jersey, where Messi exited in tears after making little impression in an ill-tempered 1-0 loss.

"I gave it my all; I have nothing left to give, and besides, there are great young players coming up who deserve their chance," Messi wrote at the time.

Before Wednesday's game, the University of Buenos Aires awarded Messi an honorary doctorate in a ceremony at the Argentine Football Association (AFA) headquarters.

Messi, who has in the past spoken of his regret at not studying more, expressed pride at the distinction.

"To be able to say that I am an honorary doctor!" he joked.

Outside the Argentina Football Association headquarters, fans unfurled a huge Argentine flag with his image inscribed "The joy of my life."

Former Barcelona teammate and Brazil's all-time top goalscorer Neymar paid tribute to the departing champion on X.

"It's not just Argentina that thanks you, the world thanks you for everything you did for football. Thank you for making me love football even more," he said.

Messi remains under contract with Inter Miami in the US's Major League Soccer league until 2028, although following the death of his father, Jorge, two months ago, he revealed he may hang up his boots for good sooner than anticipated.

Messi's departure comes four years after his greatest triumph in international football, leading Argentina to victory at the 2022 World Cup to end the country's 36-year wait for a third title, cementing his status as Diego Maradona's heir.

"I believe Messi gave everything, absolutely everything, so it doesn't bother me at all that he's leaving. He has more than earned it, let him enjoy himself, let him rest," Cecilia Adriano, 52, told a reporter from the Agence France-Presse news agency.

During his time with the Albiceleste, Argentina won one World Cup, were runners-up twice (Brazil 2014 and North America 2026) and were also crowned Copa America champions in 2021 and 2024.

title: Think you can spot scam red flags? The warning signs are changing
text:
IN BRIEF ANZ has warned businesses about sophisticated scams in upcoming busy commerce periods.

Cybersecurity experts say AI improves every stage of a scam.

Australians are being warned that some of the most common advice for spotting scams is becoming less effective, as criminals use artificial intelligence to create convincing emails, phone calls and video deepfakes.

Banks and cybersecurity experts say artificial intelligence (AI) is helping fraudsters impersonate trusted colleagues, businesses and even family members with a level of sophistication that can be almost impossible to detect.

The warning comes ahead of the Black Friday sales period and summer holidays, when scammers typically exploit heightened spending and pressure to target victims.

More than 84,000 cybercrime reports were made in 2025, while the average self-reported cost of cybercrime to businesses rose sharply, according to the Australian Signals Directorate.

How AI is changing the scam landscape

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

AI is transforming every stage of a scam, from impersonation to execution, according to Sanjay Jha, a professor at UNSW's School of Computer Science and Engineering.

"What’s genuinely new is three things: the impersonation of real, trusted people, real-time deepfakes, and the scale and personalisation that the technology brings to financial crime," he said.

AI technology allows criminals to produce deepfake videos of trusted people, including doctors, celebrities and business leaders, to promote fake products or investments. It can clone voices of family members, colleagues or executives asking for money.

The volume and quality of scam techniques are a concern, as large language models can write fluent, personalised messages in any language, with fewer spelling mistakes, and can run thousands of conversations at once.

"We used to tell people to look for spelling mistakes," Jha said, adding that advances in AI mean scammers can produce fluent, convincing messages with few obvious errors.

Scammers can appear on a live call impersonating someone else, Jha said, pointing to a 2024 case in Hong Kong, when United Kingdom engineering firm Arup transferred about HK$200m ($36.5 million) to criminals after a deepfaked multi-person conference.

"AI has turned scamming from a craft into a factory. A few seconds of your voice is now enough for a criminal to become you," he said.

Professor in CyberCrime and Cyberwar at UNSW, Richard Buckland, said any information available on the internet is accessible to criminals using AI, and that experts were "just scratching the surface" of its abilities.

"If I wanted to scam you, you might have published all sorts of stuff in your youth, your dad might have said things, your friends may have, but it's in a thousand locations, and before AI, no one would ever find it," he said

"But that's actually all inside the AI now. So AIs can access a vast amount of information about us and know about us."

AI lets criminals enact existing scams faster, at scale and more convincingly, he said, and the technology was easily accessible.

"It's really a world of outsourcing now; you could pay someone to do it, you could buy a model that does it."

The most common scams targeting businesses

The most common scams affecting businesses include the impersonation of legitimate business email accounts, known as Business Email Compromise (BEC), payment redirection scams, impersonation scams, mule accounts, identity fraud, investment scams and goods and services scams.

BEC and payment redirection scams involve criminals gaining access to or impersonating legitimate business email accounts. Victims often believe they are paying a genuine supplier or business partner, when the funds are being transferred to a fraudulent account.

Jha said scammers use AI to study a company’s public information, past emails where accounts have been compromised, and the writing style of its executives and suppliers. They then send a "perfectly worded email, in the right tone, at the right moment in a real transaction", asking to update banking details.

AI can also generate realistic fake invoices and receipts that match a supplier’s branding. "Instead of just an email, the 'CEO' now follows up with a phone call in their cloned voice, or joins a video call."

READ MORE Joseph knows how to fight scams. This one almost got to him

Similarly, scammers can pretend to be trusted organisations or individuals, including banks, suppliers or government agencies.

Impersonation scams generally rely on urgency and social conditioning to pressure victims to share information, click malicious links or approve payments or transfer funds.

One of the most significant emerging threats identified by ANZ is the use of stolen or falsified identities to open accounts that can receive scam proceeds. Known as "mule" accounts, these are used to facilitate financial crime, including money laundering.

Identity fraud was the most common scam reported in 2025, and ANZ said it has identified a "growing misuse" of mule accounts across the financial system.

Investment scams trick individuals and businesses into investing in fake or non-existent opportunities by promising attractive returns or exclusive offers. They rank consistently among the highest-loss scam categories reported to ANZ.

"AI easily produces deepfake videos of well-known business figures, journalists or politicians endorsing a trading platform, fake news articles, fake dashboards showing ‘profits’, and chatbots that keep victims engaged for weeks," Jha said.

"In short, AI removes the tell-tale signs we taught people to look for: bad grammar, a stranger’s voice, a generic greeting. The scam now looks and sounds like business as usual."

Individuals and businesses are also urged to look out for goods and services scams — advertised goods and services that are fake, misrepresented or never delivered after payment is made, commonly occurring through online marketplaces, social media platforms and fraudulent websites. While often lower in value, goods and services scams remain among the highest-volume scam types reported by ANZ.

ANZ general manager specialist sales, Cosi De Angelis, said that as AI evolved, financial crime was becoming harder to detect because it is "often hidden within legitimate businesses, trusted relationships, and everyday transactions".

"In many cases, criminals are exploiting trust as effectively as they are technology," De Angelis said.

How to defend against 'routine' scams

Jha said that scams would only become more sophisticated.

"We'll see real-time deepfake video calls become routine, AI agents that run entire scam conversations end to end, and scams that combine stolen data, cloned voices and fake documents in one coordinated attack," he said.

"It is an arms race, and criminals adapt quickly to every new defence."

Between October 2025 and June 2026, ANZ customer scam losses fell by 24 per cent compared with the same period the previous year. During that time, the bank said it also prevented and recovered more than $100 million in scam and fraud-related funds.

ANZ said it is encouraging businesses to review their cyber security practices and ensure staff understand the warning signs of cyber-enabled scams and fraud.

"Technology will continue to evolve, but human judgement remains one of the strongest defences," De Angelis said.

Jha said there was real progress being made by banks, telcos and digital platforms using AI to detect and prevent cybercrime.

"Reported losses have come down from their peak in recent years. Banks are also intercepting and recovering more stolen money than before. That shows coordinated action works," he said.

But Buckland said in the meantime, large financial institutions needed to stop contacting customers by phone and email.

"If you get an email, there's actually no way you can absolutely be sure it's the right email. And if we get a call, there's no way we can be sure we're speaking to who we think we are, even if the correct number shows on the screen.

"So companies have to stop doing it," he said.

While banks were "lucky" to have physical branches, Buxton anticipated acting against these threats would be a problem for many organisations, in a future where the only trustworthy communications would be "in-person".

"If you can only contact your customers electronically, you can no longer be distinguished from a scammer," he said.

"So how's it going to work?"

title: 'Voice of the news': Tributes continue for former SBS host Richard Morecroft

Morecroft spent almost twenty years leading the ABC's 7pm NSW news bulletin.

Former ABC News presenter and SBS host Richard Morecroft has been remembered as a generational talent.

Morecroft died "at a time of his choosing" on NSW's south coast on Tuesday, aged 70, following his cancer diagnosis earlier in 2026, his family said.

title: Coalition's 'biggest' ever migration slashing has three major issues, critic says
text:
Key Points Net overseas migration would be cut to 100,000, almost a third of current levels.

The plan flags new cuts to temporary visas for graduates, low-skill migrants and humanitarian intake.

The Coalition has pledged the "biggest cut to immigration in Australian history", slashing migrant numbers by more than 100,000.

Prioritising "high-value" migrants over family members and international students, halving humanitarian visas, while also cracking down on visa hopping and overstayers, has been branded a policy grounded on "three false premises" that could damage the economy, by a migration expert.

Coalition leader Angus Taylor says the plan will reduce temporary visa holders by around 650,000 over four years, and deliver a budget-neutral outcome while reducing overall migrant numbers by replacing lower-tax-paying temporary migrants with higher-skilled workers.

"If you have a temporary graduate visa or a student visa, on average, they’re going to give you $7,000 to $14,000 of tax income and economic contribution," Taylor said on Tuesday. "A temporary skilled visa is over $30,000."

Net overseas migration (NOM) will fall to almost a third of current levels, reducing the 3 million temporary migrants in Australia by tightening visa application pathways to stop visa-hopping by international students who use it to become temporary permanent migrants. Overseas arrivals would be linked to housing completions in Australia, which were 170,000 last year.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"We have seen under Labor our universities selling not education but visa pathways, migration pathways. That will end under this policy," Taylor said.

"We will bring in higher-skilled migrants who better meet Australia’s needs. This means prioritising skilled migration, including skilled partners and employer-sponsored applicants who meet high-quality criteria for income, age, English and full-time work."

Source: SBS News

Assuring voters the cuts to immigration would not add to skills shortages, a specialist stream of the Skills in Demand Visa will bring in up to 5,000 more highly skilled workers each year, and 15,000 Skilled Project Visas each year will be added for major projects, with workers tied to a defined project and period to plug workforce shortages.

Business groups, Labor and Greens push back

However, business groups, Labor and the Greens agree the cuts are too deep and will hurt the economy.

Property Council of Australia chief executive Mike Zorbas said the cuts will "tip a big bucket of cold water over businesses across Australia".

"Just when the Albanese government was busy proving they were best placed to tax the life out of investment in housing supply over the next year, along comes this flat tyre of a policy," Zorbas said.

"These migration cuts are just too deep for precision outcomes ... This limbo-dancing under One Nation’s migration bar will end in tears."

Greens Leader David Shoebridge told SBS News immigration policy needs to adapt for diaspora communities to connect via family reunions, a fair humanitarian intake can be matched with investments in TAFE and universities to meet Australian industry and skills needs.

“We are not going to start picking figures out of the air that fall apart at the slightest scrutiny. The proof is watching how One Nation, the Coalition and Labor have all been chopping and changing their number over the past 18 months as soon as serious scrutiny is applied," Shoebridge said.

Assistant Minister for Productivity Andrew Leigh told the ABC the proposed immigration changes will have a "huge negative impact on the economy".

The Coalition plan would virtually eliminate bridging visas. Protection visa applications will need to be made within 30 days of arrival and merit review rights for some visa refusals and character decisions will be removed.

Migration expert says plan based on 'false premises'

Changes to the temporary graduate visa were "clearly necessary", Australian National University professor Alan Gamlen, a migration expert, told SBS News.

"These were expanded for simple reasons: it doesn't make sense to have somebody come to Australia and pay to get an Australian degree, and just when they're ready to enter the labour market, having paid their own costs to get ready for it, we send them home," Gamlen said.

The visa was built for a post-pandemic labour market that was still recovering but those conditions no longer apply.

However, he said the Coalition's other changes are "One Nation lite", based on several "false premises" because countries as diverse as Austria, Czech Republic, Netherlands, and Canada face similar migration issues after their arrivals went down and then up after the pandemic.

"The (migration) policies put in place by the Coalition for very good reasons during the pandemic emergency were extended by the Labor government.. this was bipartisan, so it's not just a bipartisan problem; it's also a global problem," Gamlen said.

"Now, since the pandemic, the arrivals in aggregate have not grown. The departures have shrunk. That's the main thing that has contributed to the excess net overseas migration that we've experienced."

Cutting arrivals won't solve the problem of too few departures, but it will cause "significant harm to the economy" at the scale the Coalition is promising, he said.

Another problematic premise in their policy is the relationship between migration and housing, Gamlen said.

"Migration on the one hand ... drives demand for more housing, but migration is also partly the solution to the lack of housing because the housing construction supply chain needs more labour.

"House prices are actually going down at the moment, and that's because of something that's got nothing to do with migration."

Visa hopping led to low departures, creating a "guest worker society", a spokesperson for Taylor told SBS news.

"Our plan tackles visa hopping by requiring most temporary visa holders to apply for secondary or subsequent visa from offshore.

"Low departure rates have also been exacerbated by Labor's failure to address the over 70,000 unlawful non-citizens residing in Australia, as well as the 30,000 illegal boat arrivals Labor has failed to remove."

'Higher' migration standards

Opposition immigration spokesperson Jonathon Duniam said: "Lowering the numbers while lifting the standards isn't just a slogan".

“We’ve been putting in the work to ensure that what we announce actually won’t destroy the economy, like One Nation’s immigration plan will. And, of course, actually do something to lower the numbers. Unlike Labor’s plan," he told News24.

Nationals leader, Matt Canavan said the policy is "an Australia first migration plan".

"We’re not just a campground, we are a nation of borders, we’re not a booking.com site, and we owe Australians a living wage, not to have their salaries undermined by a cheap foreign labour force," Canavan said.

Second and third-year Working Holiday Makers will be able to reapply onshore, reversing Labor’s ballot system and caps for second- and third-year Working Holiday Maker visa extensions.

Taylor said the Coalition will differentiate between Working Holiday Makers in regional and non-regional areas by raising visa fees with an exemption for regional areas.

However, second and subsequent temporary visa applications will need to be made offshore, to reduce visa hopping.

The plan will also halve the humanitarian intake to 10,000 places a year, but remain flexible to respond to crisis needs.

What are Labor and One Nation's immigration policy alternatives?

Labor: Changes announced in September will make it harder and more expensive for international students to change visas, stop them from bringing family members and reduce backpacker numbers by 40,000 to get the NOM down to 225,000 by 2028.

Labor also announced a crackdown on visa overstayers and migration agents lodging baseless claims.

There are also reforms to the migration points system tipping the balance towards people with housing construction, healthcare, and education skills.

One Nation: After announcing a NOM figure of "about 130,000", the party settled on "negative migration", followed by an annual NOM figure of 130,000 people.

It plans to "cut immigration by over 570,000 people from current Labor levels" by capping visas at 130,000 per year to ease pressure on housing, wages, and infrastructure. And deport any visa holder who breaks the law. Introduce an eight-year waiting period for citizenship and welfare, ensuring new arrivals contribute before they take.

title: Comedian Judith Lucy announces cancer diagnosis: 'I'll be keeping you abreast'

IN BRIEF Comedian Judith Lucy has announced she will undergo a double mastectomy following a breast cancer diagnosis.

She shared the news in a joke-filled video, quipping about the ironic timing of her newly released book on wellness.

Judith Lucy has been diagnosed with breast cancer and will undergo a double mastectomy in the coming weeks.

The Australian comedian and actress announced the news in a video posted on social media on Tuesday, joking that she learned of the diagnosis shortly after receiving a faecal transplant and just before releasing her new book, Well Well Well.

"Now let's address the elephant in the room ... there's nothing like releasing a book on wellness as you're being diagnosed with breast cancer," she quipped.

She said the cancer was "relatively non-aggressive" and in its early stages, and she had decided to remove both breasts after her doctor recommended a single mastectomy.

"I have had 40 years of, if I do say so myself, large and spectacular breasts. You had your chance, fellas," she said.

title: The two-metre question that could wipe out a population
text:
IN BRIEF World leaders will spend a day on Tuvalu's main atoll as part of the pre-COP31 summit.

The summit has drawn criticism on several fronts, including the sparse turnout of leaders beyond the Pacific.

Leaders from 13 countries will join Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in Tuvalu's capital, Funafuti, today to see what rising seas are doing to one of the world's lowest-lying nations.

The country, which is made up of three islands, sits on average just two metres above sea-level, with the highest point reaching just 4.6 metres above sea-level.

The visit is the centrepiece of the pre-COP31 summit, the annual meeting at which ministers set priorities for United Nations climate negotiations.

Fiji is co-hosting the four-day gathering in Nadi with Tuvalu and Australia, a role Pacific nations secured through a compromise that gave COP31 hosting rights to Türkiye and the position of president of negotiations to Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen.

Pre-COPs are usually low-key meetings of ministers and officials, but the Australian government invited national leaders to Tuvalu to see the threat of climate change up close.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The delegation will fly more than 1,000 kilometres north from Fiji, joined by UN climate chief Simon Stiell, European Union climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra and COP31 president-designate Murat Kurum.

They will travel by canoe to inspect land raised under the Tuvalu Coastal Adaptation Project and solar projects built to cut the country's reliance on diesel, before returning to Fiji to sign a leaders' declaration.

"We ask you to come to the Pacific because some things cannot be understood from a distance," Fiji's Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka told delegates on Monday.

Sea level rise a 'present reality' for Tuvalu

NASA's Sea Level Change Team found sea levels around Tuvalu rose about 15 centimetres in the three decades to 2023 — roughly one and a half times the global average.

The team projects that much of the country's land and critical infrastructure will lie below the average high-tide mark by 2050.

Seawater is already seeping into soil and freshwater supplies, making taro and breadfruit harder to grow, while bleaching degrades the corals that sustain the country's fisheries.

"Sea-level rise is not a future threat, it is a present reality," Tuvalu Prime Minister Feleti Teo told the UN General Assembly last month.

About 60 per cent of Tuvalu's roughly 10,000 people live on Funafuti.

Under the 2023 Falepili Union treaty, Australia offers up to 280 Tuvaluans permanent residency each year.

Registrations for the first visa ballot in 2025, including family members, covered more than a third of the population.

The first recipients arrived earlier this year.

A thin international guest list

Only one national leader from outside the Pacific is expected to make the trip to the pre-COP31 event, triggering the Opposition to criticise the government over the value of the summit.

Fiji had named five leaders from beyond the region as likely attendees, but some have withdrawn, including Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul as severe flooding hit Bangkok.

Diplomats from several Western nations told Reuters they could not justify a multi-day journey with COP31 only weeks away.

READ MORE The climate question following Albanese from Palau to New York

For Vanuatu's climate minister Ralph Regenvanu, the turnout fell short: "We were hoping for more," he told Reuters.

Bowen defended the numbers, citing the president of Palau's view that "if you get one prime minister, you're doing well because prime ministers and presidents don't go to pre-COP".

Opposition energy and emissions reduction spokesperson Dan Tehan argued the low attendance showed the conference was a waste of taxpayers' money, calling it a "farce" and Bowen's "vanity project".

Hosts under scrutiny over fossil fuel records

Environmental groups and Pacific nations have both criticised the two COP31 hosts over their record on combating climate change.

The summit opened days after a NSW regulator approved a 19-year extension of the Hunter Valley Operations coal mine, the largest coal mine expansion in the state's history.

Joint owners Yancoal and Glencore estimate the extension could produce 809 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions if it wins federal approval.

In September, Regenvanu said Australia wasn't doing enough to lower greenhouse gas emissions, saying "the very least a country like Australia should be doing is stopping future expansion, and it's not doing that".

Climate Analytics chief executive Bill Hare said Labor had approved 37 fossil fuel developments for export since its election in 2022.

Using UN trade data, a 350.org report estimated Australian coal shipped to Türkiye had been responsible for more than 75 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions since 2015.

"Rather than leading the transition away, both countries are still expanding fossil fuels at extreme rates," 350.org's head of political strategy Andreas Sieber said.

Australia accounts for 25 per cent of world coal exports, ranking second behind Indonesia for total coal exports among all nations, according to the International Energy Agency.

Türkiye drew 33.6 per cent of its electricity from coal last year, according to official figures, despite a 2053 net-zero target.

In July, a Turkish court struck down environmental approval for two new units at the Afşin-Elbistan lignite plant.

A month earlier, the government announced a new 1,050-megawatt unit at the Cenal coal plant, according to campaign group Beyond Fossil Fuels.

title: UK author, former Conservative MP Jeffrey Archer dies at 86
text:
In brief Author Jeffrey Archer has died shortly before the release of his final novel.

His careers as an author and politician were marked by literary success and scandal.

Jeffrey Archer, the bestselling British novelist and former politician who was jailed for lying in a high-profile libel case, has died aged ‌86, his publisher HarperCollins said on Tuesday.

Archer sold more over 300 million copies of his books worldwide and was known for pacy thrillers ‌such as his 1976 debut Not A Penny More, Not A Penny Less and 1979's Kane & Abel. His final novel, Adam and Eve, is due to be published on Tuesday.

Kate Elton, HarperCollins' UK CEO and Archer's editor, said in a statement: "We're all devastated to have lost a writer who has brought joy to generations of readers — and a true friend."

Archer was also ‌a prominent Conservative politician, ‌who served ⁠as an MP for five years before becoming a senior party official under then-prime minister Margaret Thatcher in the mid-1980s.

But he was as well-known for his very public downfall.

Business leaders have demanded the government clarify its stance on the Australian Taxation Office’s sudden removal of credit cards as a payment method, after Labor ministers contradicted each other over the move. The tax office surprised small business owners earlier this month as the Reserve Bank of Australia’s ban on credit card surcharges came into effect. The ATO said it would stop taking credit card payments for tax bills from November 30, arguing it could not absorb the fees. Housing Minister Clare O’Neil said the government had concern’s over the ATO’s proposal. Alex Ellinghausen The ban, which Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has spruiked as a cost-of-living measure that would save households $1.6 billion a year, has incurred the wrath of small businesses and the opposition. Small Business Minister Anne Aly was the first to raise concerns over the ATO’s move on Wednesday, urging the tax office to consult more widely about the ban’s implementation. Cabinet minister Clare O’Neil weighed in on Thursday morning, saying the government had “some real concerns about what the ATO is proposing to do here”.

Advertisement

“Small businesses across the country really struggle to manage their cash flow, and I know that partly because I grew up in a household where both my mum and my dad ran their own small business,” O’Neil told Nine’s Today show. The comments put her at odds with Assistant Minister for the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton, who shortly afterwards said the government “supports the ATO’s decision” and that the tax office was ensuring consistency between the public and private sectors. Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton said there was “no reason” for businesses to raise prices because of the surcharge ban. Alex Ellinghausen “They don’t want the people who are not paying by credit card, which is 98 per cent of taxpayers, to be subsidising those that do,” Charlton told ABC radio. The confusion sparked calls from the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry for the government to show leadership and provide businesses with certainty.

Advertisement

“We want a response, and we want one clear outcome which is consistent across government,” chief executive Andrew McKellar told reporters in Canberra. “We don’t want to see agencies like the tax office going alone and acting in this way.” McKellar said while the tax office has argued the change would only affect 5 per cent of businesses, that figure represented a quarter of a million small businesses. Loading The ATO stood by its decision after meeting with stakeholders on Wednesday, in a consultation that McKellar said was fruitless.

Advertisement

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said on Thursday that Labor was “all over the shop”. Related Article Payments ‘Quite ill-prepared’: Shops scramble to meet new card surcharge ban “We’ve had the housing minister in one place, the small business minister somewhere else, and the de facto treasurer has been defending the ATO,” Taylor said. “But they should, from today, get rid of the ban, axe the ban that they’ve put on the ability of small businesses to pay tax with their credit cards.” Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson accused the government of double standards.

“The government says to small business, you’ve got to absorb these costs, but when it comes to payment systems to us, we’re not going to absorb those costs,” he told News24. In her Thursday morning interview, O’Neil backed the Reserve Bank’s call to scrap credit card fees, saying Labor’s position was that Australians should not be charged to spend their money. But she urged the ATO to find a solution for tax bills in consultation with the business sector. “Cash flow is the biggest thing that’s often of concern for small business, and using credit cards to pay tax bill is a way that a lot of people are just managing that issue,” the housing minister said. “We really want the ATO to go back and talk to business about what they’ve decided to do here and think about how they can find a solution that works.” Asked why the government was taking credit for the ban but would not resolve the problems associated with it, O’Neil said the changes were working through the system and would take time to finesse.

American author Bonnie Garmus was on the cusp of 65 when her debut novel, Lessons in Chemistry, was published – after a career in copywriting and advertising, and an astonishing 98 rejections from agents for an earlier manuscript. The story of Elizabeth Zott, a brilliant chemist who becomes the unlikely star of a TV cooking show in 1960s California, went on to become a global sensation, selling almost 10 million copies and inspiring a hit TV series starring Brie Larson. Now Garmus is back with Peck & Peck, a funny, warm-hearted romp about Batter Gray, a poetry-obsessed recent graduate who lands a job at a prestigious poetry journal in 1980s New York. For all its whimsy, the novel has plenty to say about distinctly contemporary concerns: the battle between art and commerce, the value we place on art and artists, and what happens when culture becomes a business. We spoke to Garmus about obsessions, sudden fame and why poetry might just save the world. Your characters tend to be obsessives, whether that’s about rowing, chemistry, poetry or typography. What’s taking up an unreasonable amount of brain space for you at the moment? That’s a really good question. Right now we’re about six weeks away from publication, so I’m writing a lot of articles for different magazines and things, and that’s taking up a lot of headspace. But I’m also dedicated to reading one poem a day. I’ve been doing that since 2009, and I find that evens me out. Related Article Dicey Topics

Good Weekend Sexism at work made Bonnie Garmus start writing. It sold 7 million copies What started the project of reading one poem a day? When I was in high school, about 14 or 15, I had a really good English teacher, and every day, he would read a poem out loud. It was one of the things that we loved about his class. He made us promise at the end of the school year that we would read a poem a day for the rest of our lives. He said, “It’s not because I think that you need to study this person or this form; it’s because poetry will end up saving your life. It will keep your brain fresh, it will keep your ideas open, and you will explore the world through poetry.” So we all kept the promise for at least four hours – until the school year was over – and then I never read a poem. Then one day I was driving home from work, and I heard a poem by Nikki Giovanni on the radio. It was a poem my teacher had read, and it brought tears to my eyes. I thought, “Why hadn’t I kept this promise?” I felt like my brain was starting to rot and work was overwhelming, so on that day, I decided to fulfil that promise to him and started reading a poem a day. I know it sounds kind of ridiculous, but it actually matters so much. If you don’t have time to read an entire book or a long magazine article, you have time to read a poem. It’s so complex that it will actually help you in lots of ways you don’t really realise until you start getting into it, including upping your empathy and connecting you with your heartbeat a little more often. Poetry is at the heart of your delightful second novel, Peck & Peck. Was it this routine that provided the inspiration for the book? Really, it was my unhappiness at that time with technology. This is way back, before Lessons in Chemistry. I was having a reckoning with my career and it felt like technology was moving in the wrong direction.

Advertisement

When I first started writing in the technology space for advertising, it was so interesting, innovative and full of promise. Then it seemed to be slowly sliding into something that I didn’t recognise. It was becoming more about making money instead of making what was worthwhile. I was really at a crossroads with what I was doing, and I was turning down more and more work because I didn’t feel good about what they were doing. This was way back before people talked about AI all the time and what a danger it is, but back then, we all knew about it and knew it was a danger. It was simply that people took it more seriously than they do today, and they would have never allowed it to come out as unregulated as it has. Peck & Peck follows a devoted young poet, Batter Gray, who gets a job at a prestigious, if dysfunctional, poetry journal – the titular Peck & Peck – in New York in 1983. What part of the story came to you first? It was the Peck & Peck office building. As I walk around cities – I live in England – I think more and more we see the same thing over and over. We see another Kentucky Fried Chicken, another Starbucks, or whatever. There’s this creeping conformity that’s been going on for a long time around the world where we go for the familiar, and I wanted to create a building that was unfamiliar. It’s not like [Barcelona’s] Sagrada Família, but it’s like that in the sense that there’s only one in the world. At the heart of the novel is a battle between commercial imperative and artistic integrity. Do you think those two things can ever happily coexist? I think they’ve always been at each other’s throats, but the world has become much more devoted to technology in a way that worries me. Now technology has decided that it’s going to take over the arts and do the arts for us as well. I don’t want it to do the arts for us. Technology is not an artist, and it doesn’t have the ability to do it in the same way. So I do worry a lot that this idea that technology can do everything is really misguided. There’s always been a belief – and my character believes it – that you’re supposed to get a good job as a lawyer, in accounting, or somewhere where you can make a living, and I certainly understand that [laughs]. I have two kids, and if one of them had come home and said, “I’ve decided to become a poet for my living,” I would have said, “Oh, how interesting ... but you have to do something else as well.” So yeah, there’s always this push-pull. But it turns out the arts are every bit as vital as anything else – as medicine, lawyerly work, maths or science. They’re all vital. There is something incredibly touching about your character Batter Gray’s obsession with poetry. Many of the staff who work at Peck & Peck are also obsessed. Do you think we need more people who care unreasonably deeply about the arts? Is that the antidote to the role of technology now? Yeah, I think so. It occurred to me as I was writing this book that it would be just bizarre if poetry was the one thing that ended up saving us. Poetry – the least-admired, least-read art – stepping forward and saying, “Here’s what we need to do.” The strange thing about poetry is that it’s incredibly honest, and right now we live in a very dishonest age. Before you published Lessons in Chemistry – which has gone on to become a phenomenal bestseller, with millions of copies sold worldwide and a hit TV series – you worked across all kinds of different writing. Was novel-writing always the calling? Oh, I was always doing it. You know how in Hollywood, every star has a script in their drawer? In copywriting and advertising, every copywriter and creative director has a book in their drawer. It’s not that you don’t want to do it; it’s that it doesn’t pay. You can’t survive. Ninety-nine per cent of all writers don’t make more than minimum wage.

Advertisement

I was very lucky to have a bestseller – let’s face it, we’re almost up to 10 million copies around the world now – and I am extremely lucky to have hit this. But does it happen very often? No, it doesn’t. People think I’m crazy, but I still work outside of novels. I know a Pulitzer Prize winner who still holds a full-time job because you cannot depend on this job for your security. Before Lessons in Chemistry was published, is it right that you had written a big, epic novel that attracted quite a number of rejection letters? Ninety-eight, yeah! I was going for the world record, but according to poets, 98 is amateur hour. Poets get rejected much more than that (laughs). But yeah, I kept submitting this thing, and it was a behemoth. It was 700 pages long. I hadn’t done my research, because if I had, I would have known that nobody in the world wants to publish a 700-page novel by an unknown writer. I found that out the hard way, and once I learnt that important lesson, I went shorter and wrote a completely different book. Related Article Streaming Breakout bestseller Lessons in Chemistry was destined for a Hollywood makeover Lessons in Chemistry follows the character Elizabeth Zott, who leaves her career as a chemist and starts a cooking show. At what point did you realise that this novel had become something much bigger than maybe you ever imagined? I’m embarrassed to say that it took a couple of years for me to really understand how big Lessons in Chemistry had become. Even when I had a movie deal and a series deal, it still didn’t feel real. Then it very slowly unfolded. However, it’s not like I’m recognised in public; it’s not that kind of fame. It’s just that the book did a lot better than I thought it was going to do. Did that level of success change your relationship with writing at all? No, uh-uh. I still write everything the same way as if I were working on an assignment for work, and that really works for me. It’s not so much that I need the structure of a working day, but I know that there are going to be days of failure. I know there will be days when I just don’t write well or can’t think of exactly what I want to say, and that’s OK. I will just wait, be patient, and wait for that voice to come back. For me, no, it hasn’t changed at all. We started this conversation talking about obsession. To see us out, do you know what obsession is coming next for you? I do, but I can’t tell you about it because it may change into another obsession of mine. I love to write about things that I’m passionate about, and it turns out that I’m passionate about a lot of things. Right now, I’m very passionate about poetry having a real place in our society, but more to the point, that AI is wrong for us right now and isn’t doing the job. It’s scary. People always ask, “How do you get your ideas?” I don’t know – I have too many, and I guess I’m mad about a lot of things, so they just keep cropping up! This is an edited extract from a longer conversation on Good Weekend Talks.

Mushroom is the star of the show at this light-filled and spacious restaurant, which is full of groups exploring the depth and breadth of Yunnan cuisine’s favourite ingredient.

A copper pot holds charred rice, nutty boletus mushroom, egg and sweet Yunnanese sausage. The clear and delicate broth of steam-pot chicken delivers extra nourishment via hits of goji berries, matsutake mushroom and chicken on the bone. Complement the shrooms with a heaped plate of cold braised pork ear, each textured slice cradling flakes of chilli crisp and beads of chilli oil. Or try steamed silken tofu, stirred into salted egg yolk sauce until it resembles molten cheese.

With help from staff, it’s easy to cover your table with blue-toned porcelain plates offering a mix of spicy, sour and earthy tastes. Bring a few buddies to best appreciate the feast, then finish with a cup of honeysuckle tea.

Teal MP Kate Chaney says she wants to see Australia’s AI Safety Institute better funded, as a parliamentary committee continues to probe the risks and potential rewards of embracing artificial intelligence.

Chaney, who is on the committee, told ABC News the institute only received $7.5 million a year.

WA MP Kate Chaney. Dominic Lorrimer

“Some of these AI companies are giving hundreds of millions of dollar sign-on bonuses to staff, so we’re just not in the game,” she said. “If we upskill and add resources to the institute, it means when we do put conditions on these companies, we will be able to work out whether they are complying with those conditions or not.”

Earlier today, the committee heard from tech companies OpenAI and Anthropic. They and other companies are backing strict energy consumption rules for data centres, but also said the government must hold up its end of the bargain.

title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
